status: Working convictions, not universal aesthetic laws

principles.conviction: Design relationships, not a row of attractive swatches.
principles.action: Judge every important color against its actual neighbors, at the size and amount it will occupy.
principles.conditions: A swatch is a useful starting sample, not a final composition.
principles.example: For a poster, compare the same coral title on cream and dark blue; keep the lettering size fixed so the background is the variable. For UI, review the accent inside the real button and surrounding surface.
principles.tradeoff: This can require separate tokens in light and dark themes rather than preserving one brand hex everywhere.
principles.check: Compare two contextual mockups; ask which element is read first and whether the intended relationship survives.

principles.conviction: Establish light–dark structure before multiplying hues.
principles.action: When hierarchy is unclear, separate the focal element, supporting planes and ground in lightness before adding another hue.
principles.conditions: Use especially for small type, dense interfaces and representational subjects. Equal-lightness vibration can be intentional in expressive work.
principles.example: Try an ink-dark headline, middle-value illustration and pale ground. Keep those roles while auditioning teal versus rust. A grayscale view is a diagnostic, not the final aesthetic judge.
principles.tradeoff: Flattening everything into maximum contrast can destroy atmospheric depth or quietness. Protect essential reading, not every decorative edge.
principles.check: Inspect thumbnail and grayscale structure, then return to color; measure required text pairs separately.

principles.conviction: Spend vividness and contrast where attention belongs.
principles.action: Decide what should dominate; reduce competing chroma, area or contrast elsewhere before making the focal color louder.
principles.conditions: A small vivid accent is a reliable starting option, not a universal rule. A vivid field can frame a quieter focal object.
principles.example: In an illustration, hold distant foliage in lower chroma and reserve vivid orange for a subject. In a dense tool, keep ordinary panels restrained and use a clear action accent.
principles.tradeoff: Equal high intensity can serve a deliberately exuberant or confrontational poster; use scale and placement to retain hierarchy.
principles.check: Ask whether two equally emphatic elements are meant to compete. If not, alter one variable and compare.

principles.conviction: Create a shared constraint, then choose deliberate variation.
principles.action: Begin with a limited hue family, common character or repeated accent. Add a color only when it performs a distinct job.
principles.conditions: The constraint can be hue, chroma, value or role; it need not be a fixed number of colors.
principles.example: A warm paper ground, dark brown lettering and one blue accent share restrained supporting tones while allowing a cool focal interruption. An analogous green scene can vary lightness widely without adding a complementary red.
principles.tradeoff: Too much sameness loses distinctions; a cohesive palette is not necessarily the most exciting or best-liked one.
principles.check: State what unifies the palette and what intentionally breaks that pattern. Remove one color and see whether a useful distinction is lost.

principles.conviction: A palette needs roles, proportions and placement.
principles.action: Define ground, support, focal and semantic roles before delivering tokens. Show their relative use, not just equal swatches.
principles.conditions: 60–30–10 may help an initial study; never enforce its percentages as correctness.
principles.example: A poster can use a dominant orange field and quiet cream title; the same colors may reverse roles in a reading app. Error and success colors in software must retain meaning across screens.
principles.tradeoff: A high-chroma field may fit expressive work yet make long reading or dense status displays harder to organize.
principles.check: Review the palette applied to a representative composition and, for UI, include default, hover, focus, error and disabled situations as relevant.

principles.conviction: Carry the intention across media, not an unexamined color recipe.
principles.action: State medium and color model. Proof the actual output before claiming a match or mixture.
principles.conditions: Perceptual spacing, display interpolation and pigment mixing answer different questions.
principles.example: Translate a screen palette into an acrylic study with measured test swatches, not an RGB average. A wide-gamut accent needs an evaluated sRGB alternative; print needs a proof on the intended stock.
principles.tradeoff: A lower-chroma reproduction may preserve hierarchy better than chasing an impossible saturated match.
principles.check: Record the color space for digital values and pigments/support/lighting for physical studies. Distinguish proposed from physically verified results.

principles.conviction: Use color to express an intention; test the interpretation.
principles.action: Name the desired character and audience, choose a defensible direction, then test it in context.
principles.conditions: Do not equate harmonious, beautiful, noticeable and appropriate. They are different goals.
principles.example: For a calm brand, begin with restrained chroma and a clear value range; compare with a more vivid version before deciding. Do not claim that blue automatically produces trust.
principles.tradeoff: A deliberately dissonant scheme may be the stronger expressive choice; calm is not always better.
principles.check: Ask whether it communicates the brief and which version the intended audience prefers. Report the rationale as judgment, not scientific certainty.

principles.conviction: Never purchase visual elegance by making meaning inaccessible.
principles.action: Keep essential text and functional distinctions usable; improve decorative freedom around that constraint.
principles.conditions: Measured WCAG text contrast is one check, not complete accessibility or a beauty score.
principles.example: Use a pale brand color as a surface with dark text rather than forcing pale text on white. Pair error color with a message or symbol.
principles.tradeoff: An artist may intentionally hide a form; an interface must not hide information users need.
principles.check: Run the provided checker on opaque sRGB pairs; require rendered analysis for transparency/images and non-color cues for meaningful states.
